metadata.title: Rain Hits You From the Front (Even When It Falls Straight Down)
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration, no doodle asides
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: If rain is falling perfectly straight down, why does it seem to hit you from the front when you walk?
beats.new_visual_element: Short-only question card: the driving question appears centered on screen in ink text with a crimson underline, posed before any explanation begins.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: question card faded out, blank cream background

beats.narration_text: Picture rain falling perfectly straight down. There is no wind, no angle to it. It is simply falling straight down.
beats.new_visual_element: A single slate arrow labeled v_rain falls straight down through the frame. A plain ink stick figure stands still on a ground line beneath it.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: stationary stick figure, vertical slate rain arrow above it

beats.narration_text: Now suppose you start walking. The rain has not changed at all. It is still falling straight down, exactly as before.
beats.new_visual_element: The stick figure begins walking at constant speed. A crimson arrow labeled v_walk appears at its feet, pointing in the direction of travel. The vertical rain arrow is unchanged.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: walking stick figure with crimson v_walk arrow at its feet, unchanged vertical rain arrow above

beats.narration_text: But from your own point of view, you are the one standing still, and everything else appears to move toward you instead. Subtracting your walking velocity from the rain's velocity gives the rain a new, backward horizontal component.
beats.new_visual_element: The scene splits into two panels. The left keeps the ground-frame view. The right, labeled WALKER'S FRAME, shows the same figure now stationary. A dashed crimson arrow labeled minus v_walk slides in tip-to-tail onto the vertical rain arrow, and the two combine into a single tilted teal resultant arrow labeled v_rain relative to you.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two panels: left unchanged ground frame, right shows stationary figure with tilted teal resultant rain arrow built from the vertical rain arrow plus the dashed crimson minus v_walk arrow

beats.narration_text: The faster you walk, the larger that horizontal component becomes. The rain appears to slant more and more into your face, even though its downward fall never changes.
beats.new_visual_element: In the right panel only, the construction replays three times in sequence: a slow walk, a medium jog, and a fast run. Each time, the vertical rain component stays exactly the same length while the horizontal minus v_walk arrow grows, so the resultant teal arrow tilts further forward, ending nearly horizontal.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: right panel holds the fast-run version: horizontal minus v_walk arrow long, teal resultant nearly horizontal, striking the figure's face directly

beats.narration_text: It is not the rain that changed direction. It is you. Relative velocity is simply vector addition, and walking into the rain adds an entirely new vector to the picture.
beats.new_visual_element: The fast-run frame holds: the figure leaning slightly forward, the vertical rain arrow, the horizontal minus v_walk arrow, and the teal resultant all labeled and visible, tip-to-tail. A gold-highlighted line of text beneath reads: it's just vector addition.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame: fast-run figure with all three arrows labeled tip-to-tail, gold-highlighted punchline text beneath
